docs.title: 13. Validate first boot
docs.text:
After the machine reboots, SSH into the node.

For amd64-01:

ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.61

For amd64-02:

ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.62

For amd64-03:

ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.63

Check cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --wait

cloud-init status --long

Check hostname.

hostnamectl

Check disks.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS,MODEL,SERIAL

Check network.

ip addr

ip route

docs.title: 14. Quick reference
docs.text:
Create seed for amd64-01:

./scripts/make-amd64-nocloud-seed.sh amd64-01 /dev/disk4

Create seed for amd64-02:

./scripts/make-amd64-nocloud-seed.sh amd64-02 /dev/disk4

Create seed for amd64-03:

./scripts/make-amd64-nocloud-seed.sh amd64-03 /dev/disk4

Boot argument:

autoinstall ds=nocloud

Effective mapping:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml -> CIDATA/user-data -> amd64-01
setup/cloud-config-amd64-02.yml -> CIDATA/user-data -> amd64-02
setup/cloud-config-amd64-03.yml -> CIDATA/user-data -> amd64-03

docs.title: 15. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If the installer does not autoinstall, confirm that the seed USB volume is named:

CIDATA

Confirm that the seed USB has these two files at the root:

user-data
meta-data

On macOS, after reinserting the seed USB, check:

ls -la /Volumes/CIDATA

Expected output includes:

user-data
meta-data

If the installer still does not find the seed, try this boot argument instead:

autoinstall ds=nocloud;s=/cdrom/

If that still does not work, use the HTTP NoCloud method instead of the seed USB method.

docs.title: 16. HTTP NoCloud fallback
docs.text:
From the repository root, create the amd64-01 seed files.

mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-01
cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data
cat > build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-01
local-hostname: amd64-01
EOF

Serve the seed directory over HTTP.

cd build/nocloud/amd64-01
python3 -m http.server 8080

Boot the AMD64 installer and add this boot argument.

Replace 192.168.2.100 with the IP address of the machine serving the files.

autoinstall ds=nocloud-net;s=http://192.168.2.100:8080/

docs.title: Ubuntu Installation and Node Provisioning
docs.text:
This document describes how to install Ubuntu on both Raspberry Pi arm64 nodes and amd64 bare-metal machines, apply cloud-init configuration, validate first boot, and prepare each node for cluster use.

For new installs, prefer Ubuntu 24.04 LTS unless a specific compatibility reason requires another release. Ubuntu provides Raspberry Pi preinstalled server images for modern Pi boards, and standard Ubuntu Server ISO images for amd64 machines. The Raspberry Pi preinstalled images include a cloud-init seed on the boot partition. For amd64 installs, cloud-init can be provided through autoinstall, NoCloud seed media, or post-install provisioning.

docs.title: References:
docs.text:
• Ubuntu Raspberry Pi images
  • Ubuntu Server amd64 ISO images
  • cloud-init documentation
  • Ubuntu autoinstall documentation
  • Hypriot flash utility

docs.title: Target Environment
docs.text:
Supported node types:

Node Type Architecture Install Method Boot Media Raspberry Pi 4 / Pi 5 arm64 Preinstalled Raspberry Pi image + cloud-init USB SSD or SD card Intel / AMD bare metal amd64 Ubuntu Server ISO or autoinstall SSD / NVMe

Recommended OS:

```text Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Server

arm64-01 Raspberry Pi arm64-02 Raspberry Pi arm64-03 Raspberry Pi arm64-04 Raspberry Pi arm64-05 Raspberry Pi

amd64-01 Intel / AMD bare metal amd64-02 Intel / AMD bare metal amd64-03 Intel / AMD bare metal

docs.title: Ubuntu Installation and Node Provisioning
docs.text:
This document describes how to provision the Ubuntu nodes for the Kalaxy3 / homelab Kubernetes cluster.

It supports both:

  • ARM64 Raspberry Pi nodes, using Ubuntu preinstalled Raspberry Pi server images and flash --userdata
  • AMD64 bare-metal nodes, using Ubuntu Server autoinstall with NoCloud user-data and meta-data

The important distinction is that the Raspberry Pi image is a preinstalled disk image, while the normal AMD64 Ubuntu Server download is an installer ISO. That means the ARM and AMD workflows both use cloud-init-style YAML, but they are consumed differently.

docs.title: 1. Repository layout
docs.text:
This document assumes the repository contains a setup/ directory with one cloud-init file per node.

setup/
├── cloud-config-arm64-01.yml
├── cloud-config-arm64-02.yml
├── cloud-config-arm64-03.yml
├── cloud-config-arm64-04.yml
├── cloud-config-arm64-05.yml
├── cloud-config-amd64-01.yml
├── cloud-config-amd64-02.yml
└── cloud-config-amd64-03.yml

The ARM64 files are used directly by the Raspberry Pi flashing process.

The AMD64 files are used as Ubuntu autoinstall NoCloud user-data files.

docs.title: 2. Node inventory
docs.text:
Adjust names and IP addresses if the actual hardware differs.

Node Architecture Intended role Example IP arm64-01 ARM64 Raspberry Pi Kubernetes worker/control candidate 192.168.2.51 arm64-02 ARM64 Raspberry Pi Kubernetes worker 192.168.2.52 arm64-03 ARM64 Raspberry Pi Kubernetes worker 192.168.2.53 arm64-04 ARM64 Raspberry Pi Kubernetes worker 192.168.2.54 arm64-05 ARM64 Raspberry Pi Kubernetes worker 192.168.2.55 amd64-01 AMD64 bare metal Kubernetes node / GPU-capable 192.168.2.61 amd64-02 AMD64 bare metal Kubernetes node / GPU-capable 192.168.2.62 amd64-03 AMD64 bare metal Kubernetes node / GPU-capable 192.168.2.63

docs.title: 3. Install required tools on macOS
docs.text:
The examples below assume the commands are being run from macOS.

Install Homebrew if it is not already installed.

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Install helper tools.

brew install coreutils xz wget

Install the Raspberry Pi flashing tool.

curl -L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hypriot/flash/master/$(uname -s)/flash   -o /usr/local/bin/flash

Make it executable.

chmod +x /usr/local/bin/flash

Confirm that flash is available.

flash --help

docs.title: 4. Download Ubuntu images
docs.text:
Create a local download directory.

mkdir -p ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi
mkdir -p ~/Downloads/ubuntu-amd64

Download the Ubuntu Raspberry Pi ARM64 preinstalled image.

cd ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi

wget https://cdimage.ubuntu.com/releases/24.04.4/release/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

Download the Ubuntu Server AMD64 installer ISO.

cd ~/Downloads/ubuntu-amd64

wget https://releases.ubuntu.com/24.04.4/ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso

The ARM64 file is a preinstalled disk image.

The AMD64 file is an installer ISO.

That difference is why the provisioning commands are different.

docs.title: 5. ARM64 Raspberry Pi provisioning model
docs.text:
For Raspberry Pi nodes, use the Ubuntu preinstalled server image and inject each node's cloud-init file with flash --userdata.

This works because the Raspberry Pi image is already a bootable installed operating system image. The flash tool writes the image to the target disk and injects the selected cloud-init config.

docs.title: 5.1 List disks before inserting the target SSD or SD card
docs.text:
diskutil list

Insert the target SSD or SD card, then list disks again.

diskutil list

Identify the new external disk.

Example:

/dev/disk3 (external, physical)

Do not use /dev/disk0. That is normally the Mac internal disk.

docs.title: 5.2 Flash arm64-01
docs.text: flash   --userdata setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml   ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

docs.title: 5.3 Flash arm64-02
docs.text: flash   --userdata setup/cloud-config-arm64-02.yml   ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

docs.title: 5.4 Flash arm64-03
docs.text: flash   --userdata setup/cloud-config-arm64-03.yml   ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

docs.title: 5.5 Flash arm64-04
docs.text: flash   --userdata setup/cloud-config-arm64-04.yml   ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

docs.title: 5.6 Flash arm64-05
docs.text: flash   --userdata setup/cloud-config-arm64-05.yml   ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

docs.title: 5.7 Boot each Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
After flashing:

  1. Eject the disk from macOS.
  2. Insert it into the Raspberry Pi.
  3. Connect Ethernet.
  4. Power on the Pi.
  5. Wait for first boot and cloud-init to complete.

Cloud-init may take several minutes during first boot.

docs.title: 6. AMD64 bare-metal provisioning model
docs.text:
For AMD64 nodes, do not use the Raspberry Pi flash --userdata command against the AMD64 installer ISO.

This is the wrong model:

flash   --userdata setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml   ~/Downloads/ubuntu-amd64/ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso

The normal AMD64 Ubuntu Server image is an installer ISO, not a preinstalled disk image. The installer needs to consume cloud-init through Ubuntu autoinstall using the NoCloud datasource.

The AMD64 files are still used, but they are used as NoCloud user-data.

docs.title: 7. AMD64 option A: installer ISO plus seed USB
docs.text:
This is the simplest and clearest AMD64 method.

You boot the machine from the normal Ubuntu Server ISO, and you attach a second USB drive containing the autoinstall seed data.

The seed USB contains:

user-data
meta-data

For each AMD64 node, the user-data file is copied from the matching generated cloud config.

docs.title: 7.1 Create a seed directory for amd64-01
docs.text:
Run this from the repository root.

mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-01

Copy the node-specific config into the NoCloud seed directory.

cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data

Create the metadata file.

cat > build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-01
local-hostname: amd64-01
EOF

docs.title: 7.2 Create a seed directory for amd64-02
docs.text:
mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-02

cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-02.yml build/nocloud/amd64-02/user-data

cat > build/nocloud/amd64-02/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-02
local-hostname: amd64-02
EOF

docs.title: 7.3 Create a seed directory for amd64-03
docs.text:
mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-03

cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-03.yml build/nocloud/amd64-03/user-data

cat > build/nocloud/amd64-03/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-03
local-hostname: amd64-03
EOF

docs.title: 8. Write a NoCloud seed USB on macOS
docs.text:
Use a small USB drive for the seed media.

The seed drive can be very small. It only needs to hold user-data and meta-data.

docs.title: 8.1 Identify the seed USB
docs.text:
Before inserting the seed USB:

diskutil list

Insert the seed USB and run:

diskutil list

Identify the new external disk.

Example:

/dev/disk4 (external, physical)

docs.title: 8.2 Erase the seed USB
docs.text:
Replace /dev/disk4 with the actual seed USB device.

diskutil eraseDisk FAT32 CIDATA MBR /dev/disk4

The volume name CIDATA is important. NoCloud commonly expects the seed volume label to be CIDATA.

docs.title: 8.3 Mount location
docs.text:
After formatting, macOS should mount it here:

/Volumes/CIDATA

Confirm it mounted.

ls /Volumes/CIDATA

docs.title: 8.4 Copy amd64-01 seed files
docs.text:
To prepare the seed USB for amd64-01:

cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

docs.title: 8.5 Copy amd64-02 seed files
docs.text:
To reuse the same seed USB for amd64-02, reinsert it and replace the files.

cp build/nocloud/amd64-02/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-02/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

docs.title: 8.6 Copy amd64-03 seed files
docs.text:
To reuse the same seed USB for amd64-03, reinsert it and replace the files.

cp build/nocloud/amd64-03/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-03/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

docs.title: 9. Boot AMD64 installer with NoCloud autoinstall
docs.text:
For each AMD64 machine:

  1. Insert the Ubuntu Server AMD64 installer USB.
  2. Insert the NoCloud seed USB labeled CIDATA.
  3. Boot the machine from the Ubuntu Server installer USB.
  4. At the GRUB menu, edit the boot entry.
  5. Add the autoinstall datasource argument to the Linux command line.

The kernel command line should include:

autoinstall ds=nocloud

Depending on the installer behavior, this variant may be needed:

autoinstall ds=nocloud;s=/cdrom/

Or this variant if the seed is mounted separately:

autoinstall ds=nocloud;s=file:///cdrom/

The exact mount path can vary depending on the machine and installer environment. The key idea is that the installer must see a NoCloud datasource containing:

user-data
meta-data

on the CIDATA volume.

docs.title: 10. AMD64 option B: serve NoCloud data over HTTP
docs.text:
Instead of using a second USB seed drive, you can serve each node's user-data and meta-data over HTTP from another machine on the LAN.

From the repository root, serve the NoCloud directory.

cd build/nocloud/amd64-01

python3 -m http.server 8080

Then boot the AMD64 installer with:

autoinstall ds=nocloud-net;s=http://192.168.2.100:8080/

Replace 192.168.2.100 with the IP address of the machine running the HTTP server.

For amd64-02:

cd build/nocloud/amd64-02

python3 -m http.server 8080

Use:

autoinstall ds=nocloud-net;s=http://192.168.2.100:8080/

For amd64-03:

cd build/nocloud/amd64-03

python3 -m http.server 8080

Use:

autoinstall ds=nocloud-net;s=http://192.168.2.100:8080/

Only run one of these simple HTTP servers at a time on the same port.

docs.title: 11. AMD64 option C: build a custom autoinstall ISO
docs.text:
This option embeds the NoCloud data directly into a custom Ubuntu Server ISO.

Use this if you want one bootable ISO per AMD64 node and do not want a second seed USB.

High-level flow:

  1. Extract the Ubuntu Server ISO.
  2. Add user-data and meta-data.
  3. Modify the boot menu to include autoinstall ds=nocloud.
  4. Rebuild the ISO.
  5. Write the rebuilt ISO to USB.

This is cleaner for repeat installs, but more work than the seed USB approach.

For this cluster, the recommended path is:

ARM64 Raspberry Pi nodes: flash --userdata
AMD64 bare-metal nodes: Ubuntu autoinstall with NoCloud seed USB

docs.title: 12. Verify first boot
docs.text:
After a node boots, wait a few minutes for cloud-init to finish.

Then SSH into the node.

Example for arm64-01:

ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.51

Example for amd64-01:

ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.61

Check hostname.

hostnamectl

Check cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --long

Check storage devices.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS,MODEL

Check network address.

ip addr

Check default route.

ip route

docs.title: 13. Validate MinIO data disk selection
docs.text:
The node configs should avoid assuming that Linux drive order is stable.

Do not assume:

/dev/sda
/dev/sdb
/dev/nvme0n1

will always appear in the same order.

The safer pattern is to detect the intended MinIO disk by durable characteristics such as:

  • rotational HDD status
  • size
  • exclusion of the boot disk
  • explicit operator confirmation where needed

After first boot, confirm the intended MinIO disk.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS,MODEL,SERIAL

Look for the 1 TB HDD intended for MinIO.

Check mounted filesystems.

df -h

Check block IDs.

sudo blkid

docs.title: 14. Confirm package installation
docs.text:
Check that common packages were installed.

which curl
which wget
which git
which jq
which yq

Check NFS and iSCSI support.

systemctl status open-iscsi --no-pager

dpkg -l | grep -E 'nfs-common|open-iscsi'

docs.title: 15. Confirm SSH access
docs.text:
From the Mac or admin workstation, test each node.

ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.51 hostname
ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.52 hostname
ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.53 hostname
ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.54 hostname
ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.55 hostname
ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.61 hostname
ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.62 hostname
ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.63 hostname

docs.title: 16. Confirm GPU visibility on AMD64 nodes
docs.text:
On AMD64 nodes with NVIDIA GPUs, confirm PCI visibility first.

lspci | grep -i nvidia

Check recommended Ubuntu drivers.

ubuntu-drivers devices

Install the recommended driver if the cloud-init file did not already do it.

Example:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y nvidia-driver-580
sudo reboot

After reboot:

nvidia-smi

docs.title: 17.1 Disk Utility shows only ESP or tiny partitions
docs.text:
In macOS Disk Utility:

  1. Click View.
  2. Select Show All Devices.
  3. Select the top-level physical disk.
  4. Erase the whole device, not just the tiny ESP partition.

Terminal is often clearer.

diskutil list

Erase the correct external device only.

Example:

diskutil eraseDisk ExFAT USBSTICK GPT /dev/disk3

Do not erase /dev/disk0.

docs.title: 17.2 Cloud-init still running
docs.text:
Check status.

cloud-init status --long

Watch logs.

sudo tail -f /var/log/cloud-init.log

sudo tail -f /var/log/cloud-init-output.log

docs.title: 17.3 SSH does not work
docs.text:
Check whether the node responds.

ping 192.168.2.51

Check SSH port.

nc -vz 192.168.2.51 22

Try verbose SSH.

ssh -vvv dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.51

docs.title: 17.4 AMD64 installer does not pick up autoinstall
docs.text:
Confirm the seed USB has exactly these files at the root:

user-data
meta-data

Confirm the volume label is:

CIDATA

On macOS, confirm with:

diskutil list

Recreate the seed USB if needed.

diskutil eraseDisk FAT32 CIDATA MBR /dev/disk4

Then copy files again.

cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

docs.title: 17.5 AMD64 installer asks questions instead of running unattended
docs.text:
That usually means one of these is wrong:

  • autoinstall was not added to the boot command line
  • the NoCloud datasource was not found
  • user-data is invalid
  • meta-data is missing
  • the seed volume is not labeled CIDATA
  • the YAML file is cloud-init only but not valid Ubuntu autoinstall format

Validate YAML before trying again.

python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import yaml

for path in Path("setup").glob("cloud-config-*.yml"):
    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        yaml.safe_load(file)
    print(f"OK: {path}")
PY

If PyYAML is missing:

python3 -m pip install pyyaml

docs.title: 18. Summary
docs.text:
Use this workflow:

ARM64 Raspberry Pi:
  Ubuntu preinstalled Raspberry Pi image
  flash --userdata setup/cloud-config-arm64-XX.yml image.img.xz

AMD64 bare metal:
  Ubuntu Server AMD64 installer ISO
  Ubuntu autoinstall
  NoCloud seed USB or NoCloud HTTP datasource
  setup/cloud-config-amd64-XX.yml copied as user-data

The AMD64 cloud-init files are not unused. They are used differently because AMD64 installation normally starts from an installer ISO, while the Raspberry Pi installation starts from a preinstalled disk image.

docs.title: ARM64
docs.text: flash   --userdata setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml   ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

docs.title: AMD64 seed USB preparation
docs.text:
mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-01
cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data
cat > build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-01
local-hostname: amd64-01
EOF

diskutil eraseDisk FAT32 CIDATA MBR /dev/disk4

cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

docs.title: AMD64 installer boot argument
docs.text:
autoinstall ds=nocloud

or:

autoinstall ds=nocloud-net;s=http://192.168.2.100:8080/

docs.title: Ubuntu Installation and Node Provisioning
docs.text:
This guide describes how to provision Ubuntu nodes for a mixed-architecture homelab or Kubernetes cluster. It supports both Raspberry Pi arm64 machines and Intel/AMD amd64 bare-metal machines.

The goal is to produce repeatable Ubuntu installs while avoiding the two most common provisioning mistakes:

  1. Flashing or installing to the wrong disk.
  2. Assuming Linux disk ordering is stable.

For new installs, prefer Ubuntu 24.04 LTS unless a specific project requires a different release. Raspberry Pi nodes use Ubuntu's preinstalled Raspberry Pi server image. Bare-metal amd64 nodes use the standard Ubuntu Server installer ISO.

This document assumes the flashing workstation is macOS.

All commands are shown in fenced code blocks so they can be selected and copied directly from a browser.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• 1. Supported Node Types
  • 2. General Safety Rules
  • 3. Recommended Repository Layout
  • 4. Raspberry Pi arm64 Provisioning
  • 5. amd64 Bare-Metal Provisioning
  • 6. amd64 Cloud-Init and Autoinstall Mapping
  • 7. First-Boot Validation for All Nodes
  • 8. Storage Validation for MinIO Nodes
  • 9. Troubleshooting
  • 10. Recommended Current Workflows
  • 11. Archived Historical Notes
  • Appendix A: Useful Validation Commands
  • Appendix B: Publishing Notes

docs.title: 1. Supported Node Types
docs.text:
This provisioning guide supports two node families.

Node Type Architecture Install Method Boot Media Raspberry Pi 4 / Pi 5 arm64 Ubuntu Raspberry Pi preinstalled image plus cloud-init USB SSD or SD card Intel / AMD bare metal amd64 Ubuntu Server ISO or autoinstall SSD or NVMe

Example cluster layout:

arm64-01  Raspberry Pi
arm64-02  Raspberry Pi
arm64-03  Raspberry Pi
arm64-04  Raspberry Pi
arm64-05  Raspberry Pi

amd64-01  Intel / AMD bare metal
amd64-02  Intel / AMD bare metal
amd64-03  Intel / AMD bare metal

Recommended operating system:

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Server

docs.title: 2. General Safety Rules
docs.text:
Provisioning writes directly to disks. Treat every flashing, imaging, and installer step as destructive until proven otherwise.

Never assume any of the following device names are stable:

/dev/disk3
/dev/sda
/dev/sdb
/dev/nvme0n1

These names can change depending on boot order, attached USB devices, drive controllers, BIOS behavior, and kernel discovery order.

Before writing an image, always identify the target disk by:

size
model
vendor
serial number
connection type
whether it appeared after insertion
whether it is removable

For MinIO or other data disks, never rely only on /dev/sda or /dev/sdb. Identify the intended disk using durable characteristics such as:

rotational status
size
model
serial number
existing filesystems
mount status
whether it contains the root filesystem
operator confirmation

docs.title: 3. Recommended Repository Layout
docs.text:
A recommended repository layout is shown below.

setup/
  cloud-config-arm64-01.yml
  cloud-config-arm64-02.yml
  cloud-config-arm64-03.yml
  cloud-config-arm64-04.yml
  cloud-config-arm64-05.yml

  autoinstall-amd64-01/
    user-data
    meta-data

  autoinstall-amd64-02/
    user-data
    meta-data

  autoinstall-amd64-03/
    user-data
    meta-data

docs/
  ubuntu-node-provisioning.md

The arm64 files are intended for Raspberry Pi nodes. The amd64 autoinstall directories are optional and should only be used once disk selection has been tested carefully.

docs.title: 4. Raspberry Pi arm64 Provisioning
docs.text:
Use this section for Raspberry Pi nodes.

Raspberry Pi provisioning uses the Ubuntu preinstalled server image for Raspberry Pi. The cloud-init configuration is injected into the image during flashing.

docs.title: 4.1 Install the Flash Tool on macOS
docs.text:
The Hypriot flash utility can write Ubuntu images and inject a cloud-init user-data file during the flashing process.

Download the flash utility.

curl -LO "https://github.com/hypriot/flash/releases/download/2.5.1/flash"

Make the downloaded file executable.

chmod +x flash

Move the executable into /usr/local/bin.

sudo mv flash /usr/local/bin/flash

Verify that the tool is available.

flash --version

If the command is not found, confirm that /usr/local/bin is in your shell PATH.

echo "$PATH"

docs.title: 4.2 Download the Ubuntu Raspberry Pi Image
docs.text:
Create a local download directory for Raspberry Pi images.

mkdir -p ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi

Move into the download directory.

cd ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi

Download the Ubuntu Raspberry Pi arm64 server image.

curl -LO "https://cdimage.ubuntu.com/releases/noble/release/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz"

Download the checksum file from the same release directory.

curl -LO "https://cdimage.ubuntu.com/releases/noble/release/SHA256SUMS"

The image file should remain compressed as .img.xz. The flash tool can use the compressed image directly.

docs.title: 4.3 Verify the Raspberry Pi Image
docs.text:
Generate the local SHA-256 checksum.

shasum -a 256 ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

Show the expected checksum from Ubuntu's SHA256SUMS file.

grep "ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz" SHA256SUMS

The value from shasum should match the value shown by grep.

Do not flash the image if the checksum does not match.

docs.title: 4.4 Identify the Target Disk on macOS
docs.text:
Before inserting the SD card or USB boot drive, list the disks currently attached to the Mac.

diskutil list

Insert the SD card or USB boot drive.

Then list the disks again.

diskutil list

Identify the newly added disk by comparing the two command outputs.

Example target disk:

/dev/disk3

Do not assume your target disk is /dev/disk3. The correct disk may be /dev/disk2, /dev/disk4, or another value.

The disk shown by flash must match the disk you identified with diskutil list.

docs.title: 4.5 Select the Correct arm64 Cloud-Init File
docs.text:
Use the cloud-init file that matches the Raspberry Pi node being provisioned.

setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml  -> arm64-01
setup/cloud-config-arm64-02.yml  -> arm64-02
setup/cloud-config-arm64-03.yml  -> arm64-03
setup/cloud-config-arm64-04.yml  -> arm64-04
setup/cloud-config-arm64-05.yml  -> arm64-05

Before flashing, inspect the selected file and confirm that the hostname, network settings, users, and SSH keys are correct.

grep -E "hostname|fqdn|192\.168\.2|users|ssh_authorized_keys" \
  setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml

If this command does not show the expected node identity, stop and check the cloud-init file before flashing.

docs.title: 4.6 Flash the Raspberry Pi Boot Device
docs.text:
The following example flashes arm64-01.

flash \
  --userdata setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml \
  ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

During flashing, the tool may prompt for confirmation.

Example prompt:

Is /dev/disk3 correct?

Only answer y if the displayed disk is definitely the intended SD card or USB boot drive.

y

If the disk is not correct, answer n or terminate the command.

docs.title: 4.7 Boot the Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
After flashing completes:

  1. Eject the boot device from macOS.
  2. Insert the SD card or USB drive into the Raspberry Pi.
  3. Connect Ethernet.
  4. Connect power.
  5. Wait for first boot and cloud-init to complete.

The first boot may take several minutes because Ubuntu expands the filesystem, applies cloud-init, configures networking, creates users, installs packages, and starts services.

docs.title: 5. amd64 Bare-Metal Provisioning
docs.text:
Use this section for Intel or AMD bare-metal machines.

The amd64 workflow uses the normal Ubuntu Server installer ISO plus the node-specific cloud-init/autoinstall file.

For amd64-01, the provisioning file is:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml

For amd64-02, the provisioning file is:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-02.yml

For amd64-03, the provisioning file is:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-03.yml

The amd64 ISO is an installer ISO, not a preinstalled disk image. That means the Raspberry Pi command pattern below is not used for amd64 machines:

flash \
  --userdata setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml \
  ~/Downloads/ubuntu-amd64/ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso

Instead, the matching setup/cloud-config-amd64-NN.yml file is copied to a NoCloud seed as user-data, and the Ubuntu installer consumes it during autoinstall.

docs.title: 5.1 Download the Ubuntu Server amd64 ISO
docs.text:
Create a local download directory for the Ubuntu Server ISO.

mkdir -p ~/Downloads/ubuntu-amd64

Move into the download directory.

cd ~/Downloads/ubuntu-amd64

Download the Ubuntu Server amd64 ISO.

curl -LO "https://releases.ubuntu.com/noble/ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso"

Download the checksum file.

curl -LO "https://releases.ubuntu.com/noble/SHA256SUMS"

Download the signed checksum file.

curl -LO "https://releases.ubuntu.com/noble/SHA256SUMS.gpg"

docs.title: 5.2 Verify the amd64 ISO
docs.text:
Generate the local SHA-256 checksum.

shasum -a 256 ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso

Show the expected checksum from Ubuntu's SHA256SUMS file.

grep "ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso" SHA256SUMS

The value from shasum should match the value shown by grep.

docs.title: 5.3 Create the Ubuntu Server Installer USB
docs.text:
Insert the USB drive that will become the Ubuntu installer.

List attached disks before and after insertion.

diskutil list

Unmount the USB installer disk.

Replace /dev/disk3 with the disk you identified.

diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk3

Write the Ubuntu Server ISO to the USB drive.

Replace /dev/rdisk3 with the raw disk path that corresponds to your target disk. On macOS, /dev/rdisk3 is the raw version of /dev/disk3.

cd ~/Downloads/ubuntu-amd64

sudo dd \
  if=ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso \
  of=/dev/rdisk3 \
  bs=4m \
  status=progress

Flush pending writes.

sync

Eject the USB installer.

diskutil eject /dev/disk3

docs.title: 5.4 Create the amd64-01 NoCloud Seed USB
docs.text:
Use a second small USB drive as the NoCloud seed device.

The seed USB must contain these two files at the root:

user-data
meta-data

For amd64-01, user-data is created from:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml

Create a local seed build directory.

mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-01

Copy the amd64-01 cloud-init/autoinstall file as user-data.

cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data

Create meta-data.

cat > build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-01
local-hostname: amd64-01
EOF

Insert the seed USB and identify it.

diskutil list

Format the seed USB with the required NoCloud label.

Replace /dev/disk4 with the seed USB disk.

diskutil eraseDisk FAT32 CIDATA MBR /dev/disk4

Copy the seed files to the USB.

cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

docs.title: 5.5 Create the amd64-02 NoCloud Seed USB
docs.text:
Reuse the same seed USB, but replace the files with the amd64-02 files.

Create the seed directory.

mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-02

Copy the amd64-02 cloud-init/autoinstall file as user-data.

cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-02.yml build/nocloud/amd64-02/user-data

Create meta-data.

cat > build/nocloud/amd64-02/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-02
local-hostname: amd64-02
EOF

Insert the seed USB and confirm it mounted as CIDATA.

ls /Volumes/CIDATA

Copy the seed files to the USB.

cp build/nocloud/amd64-02/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-02/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

docs.title: 5.6 Create the amd64-03 NoCloud Seed USB
docs.text:
Reuse the same seed USB, but replace the files with the amd64-03 files.

Create the seed directory.

mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-03

Copy the amd64-03 cloud-init/autoinstall file as user-data.

cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-03.yml build/nocloud/amd64-03/user-data

Create meta-data.

cat > build/nocloud/amd64-03/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-03
local-hostname: amd64-03
EOF

Insert the seed USB and confirm it mounted as CIDATA.

ls /Volumes/CIDATA

Copy the seed files to the USB.

cp build/nocloud/amd64-03/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-03/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

docs.title: 5.7 Boot amd64 with Autoinstall
docs.text:
For the target AMD64 node:

  1. Insert the Ubuntu Server AMD64 installer USB.
  2. Insert the NoCloud seed USB labeled CIDATA.
  3. Boot the machine from the Ubuntu Server installer USB.
  4. At the GRUB menu, edit the boot entry.
  5. Add the autoinstall argument to the Linux kernel command line.

Use this boot argument first:

autoinstall ds=nocloud

If the installer does not find the seed, use the explicit seed path variant:

autoinstall ds=nocloud;s=/cdrom/

The installer should read:

/Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
/Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data

from the seed USB and run the matching node config.

For amd64-01, that means it runs:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml

as the NoCloud user-data.

docs.title: 5.8 Provision amd64-01
docs.text:
Prepare the seed USB with the amd64-01 files.

mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-01
cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data
cat > build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-01
local-hostname: amd64-01
EOF

diskutil eraseDisk FAT32 CIDATA MBR /dev/disk4

cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-01/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

Boot the target machine with the Ubuntu Server installer USB and this seed USB.

At the installer GRUB line, include:

autoinstall ds=nocloud

docs.title: 5.9 Provision amd64-02
docs.text:
Prepare the seed USB with the amd64-02 files.

mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-02
cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-02.yml build/nocloud/amd64-02/user-data
cat > build/nocloud/amd64-02/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-02
local-hostname: amd64-02
EOF

diskutil eraseDisk FAT32 CIDATA MBR /dev/disk4

cp build/nocloud/amd64-02/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-02/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

Boot the target machine with the Ubuntu Server installer USB and this seed USB.

At the installer GRUB line, include:

autoinstall ds=nocloud

docs.title: 5.10 Provision amd64-03
docs.text:
Prepare the seed USB with the amd64-03 files.

mkdir -p build/nocloud/amd64-03
cp setup/cloud-config-amd64-03.yml build/nocloud/amd64-03/user-data
cat > build/nocloud/amd64-03/meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: amd64-03
local-hostname: amd64-03
EOF

diskutil eraseDisk FAT32 CIDATA MBR /dev/disk4

cp build/nocloud/amd64-03/user-data /Volumes/CIDATA/user-data
cp build/nocloud/amd64-03/meta-data /Volumes/CIDATA/meta-data
sync
diskutil eject /Volumes/CIDATA

Boot the target machine with the Ubuntu Server installer USB and this seed USB.

At the installer GRUB line, include:

autoinstall ds=nocloud

docs.title: 6. amd64 Cloud-Init and Autoinstall Mapping
docs.text:
The amd64 cloud-init files are part of the provisioning flow.

They are not optional manual references. They are the node-specific autoinstall/NoCloud user-data inputs.

setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml  -> amd64-01 user-data
setup/cloud-config-amd64-02.yml  -> amd64-02 user-data
setup/cloud-config-amd64-03.yml  -> amd64-03 user-data

The generated NoCloud seed layout is:

build/nocloud/amd64-01/
  user-data
  meta-data

build/nocloud/amd64-02/
  user-data
  meta-data

build/nocloud/amd64-03/
  user-data
  meta-data

The installer consumes the selected seed at boot time.

For amd64-01, the effective provisioning path is:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml
  -> build/nocloud/amd64-01/user-data
  -> CIDATA/user-data
  -> Ubuntu Server autoinstall
  -> provisioned amd64-01 machine

For amd64-02, the effective provisioning path is:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-02.yml
  -> build/nocloud/amd64-02/user-data
  -> CIDATA/user-data
  -> Ubuntu Server autoinstall
  -> provisioned amd64-02 machine

For amd64-03, the effective provisioning path is:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-03.yml
  -> build/nocloud/amd64-03/user-data
  -> CIDATA/user-data
  -> Ubuntu Server autoinstall
  -> provisioned amd64-03 machine

docs.title: 7. First-Boot Validation for All Nodes
docs.text:
Run these checks after the first boot on both arm64 and amd64 machines.

These steps confirm that the node is reachable, correctly named, running the expected OS, and using the expected disks.

docs.title: 7.1 Check Network Reachability
docs.text:
Ping the node by IP address.

ping <node-ip>

Example:

ping 192.168.2.51

If the node does not respond, confirm Ethernet, DHCP or static IP configuration, switch connectivity, and whether the machine completed first boot.

docs.title: 7.2 SSH into the Node
docs.text:
Connect with SSH.

ssh dbuddenbaum@<node-ip>

Example:

ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.51

If SSH fails, confirm that OpenSSH was installed and that cloud-init completed.

docs.title: 7.3 Check Cloud-Init Status
docs.text:
Wait for cloud-init to finish.

cloud-init status --wait

Show detailed cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --long

Cloud-init should report that it is done. If it reports an error, review the cloud-init logs before continuing.

docs.title: 7.4 Check Hostname
docs.text:
Show the active hostname and operating system identity.

hostnamectl

Confirm that the hostname matches the expected node name.

Examples:

arm64-01
arm64-02
amd64-01
amd64-02

docs.title: 7.5 Check IP Addresses and Routes
docs.text:
Show assigned IP addresses.

ip addr

Show the routing table.

ip route

Confirm that the node has the expected static IP or DHCP-assigned IP and that a default route exists.

docs.title: 7.6 Check OS Version
docs.text:
Show the Ubuntu release.

lsb_release -a

The release should match the expected Ubuntu version for the cluster.

docs.title: 7.7 Check Block Devices
docs.text:
List block devices with size, rotational status, filesystem, mountpoint, model, and serial number.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL

This is one of the most important validation commands. Use it to confirm which disk is the boot disk and which disk is the candidate MinIO or data disk.

docs.title: 7.8 Check Mounted Filesystems
docs.text:
Show mounted filesystems and available space.

df -h

Confirm that the root filesystem is mounted on the expected boot device.

docs.title: 7.9 Check SSH Service
docs.text:
Show the SSH service status.

systemctl status ssh --no-pager

The service should be active and running.

docs.title: 8. Storage Validation for MinIO Nodes
docs.text:
Before formatting or mounting a MinIO disk, confirm that the selected disk is not the boot disk.

This matters for both Raspberry Pi and amd64 nodes.

Expected storage pattern:

Raspberry Pi nodes:
  boot device: USB SSD or SD card
  MinIO disk: 1 TB HDD

amd64 nodes:
  boot device: SSD or NVMe
  MinIO disk: 1 TB HDD

docs.title: 8.1 Identify the Root Filesystem
docs.text:
Show the mounted root filesystem.

findmnt /

Example output:

TARGET SOURCE         FSTYPE OPTIONS
/      /dev/nvme0n1p2 ext4   rw,relatime

The parent disk of the root filesystem must not be used for MinIO.

In this example, /dev/nvme0n1 is the parent disk of /dev/nvme0n1p2, so /dev/nvme0n1 is the boot disk.

docs.title: 8.2 List Candidate Data Disks
docs.text:
List whole disks without partitions.

lsblk -dn -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,MODEL,SERIAL

Look for the expected MinIO disk by size, rotational status, model, and serial number.

docs.title: 8.3 Show Filesystems
docs.text:
Show existing filesystems.

lsblk -f

A candidate MinIO disk should not contain the active root filesystem.

If a disk already contains data, stop and confirm whether it should be reused, wiped, or excluded.

docs.title: 8.4 Safe MinIO Disk Rule
docs.text:
A disk is a candidate MinIO disk only if all of the following are true:

it is not the root disk
it is the expected size
it is not already mounted
it does not contain the OS filesystem
it matches expected rotational or model characteristics
the operator confirms it

Do not format any disk unless these checks pass.

docs.title: 8.5 Example Manual Confirmation
docs.text:
Use lsblk to inspect the machine.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL

Use findmnt to identify the root filesystem.

findmnt /

Use df to confirm mounted filesystems.

df -h

Only after the boot disk and MinIO disk are clearly identified should a formatting or mounting step be allowed.

docs.title: 9. Troubleshooting
docs.text: This section covers common provisioning failures.

docs.title: 9.1 Cannot SSH into the Node
docs.text:
Check whether the node responds to ping.

ping <node-ip>

Check whether port 22 is reachable.

nc -vz <node-ip> 22

If ping works but SSH fails, check the SSH service from the node console.

sudo systemctl status ssh --no-pager

Check SSH logs.

sudo journalctl -u ssh --no-pager

Check cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --long

Common causes:

cloud-init did not finish
OpenSSH server was not installed
wrong username
wrong SSH key
wrong static IP configuration
node is on the wrong network

docs.title: 9.2 Cloud-Init Did Not Finish
docs.text:
Check cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --long

Check cloud-init service logs.

sudo journalctl -u cloud-init --no-pager

Check final-stage cloud-init logs.

sudo journalctl -u cloud-final --no-pager

Cloud-init issues usually come from YAML formatting errors, package install failures, network configuration errors, or commands in runcmd that failed.

docs.title: 9.3 Wrong Hostname or IP Address
docs.text:
Check the active hostname.

hostnamectl

Check IP addresses.

ip addr

Check routes.

ip route

Check netplan.

cat /etc/netplan/*.yaml

On the provisioning workstation, check the cloud-init file that was used.

grep -E "hostname|fqdn|addresses|gateway4|nameservers" \
  setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml

If the wrong cloud-init file was flashed, reflash the node with the correct file.

docs.title: 9.4 Wrong Disk Was Selected
docs.text:
If the wrong disk may have been selected, stop immediately before formatting, mounting, or installing anything else.

Inspect all block devices.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL

Identify the mounted root filesystem.

findmnt /

Check mounted filesystems.

df -h

Do not continue until the root disk and intended data disk are clearly identified.

docs.title: 9.5 Raspberry Pi Does Not Boot from USB
docs.text:
Check the following:

  1. The Raspberry Pi model supports USB boot.
  2. The EEPROM or bootloader is current.
  3. The USB drive is powered correctly.
  4. The image was flashed to the correct device.
  5. Ethernet is connected.
  6. Power is stable.
  7. A monitor shows boot activity.

For Raspberry Pi 4 and newer, USB boot should be handled through the Raspberry Pi bootloader settings. Do not rely on disk-number tricks from the flashing host.

docs.title: 10. Recommended Current Workflows
docs.text: This section summarizes the preferred provisioning path for each node type.

docs.title: 10.1 Raspberry Pi arm64 Node Workflow
docs.text:
Use this workflow for each Raspberry Pi node.

  1. Select the correct setup/cloud-config-arm64-NN.yml file.
  2. Download the Ubuntu Raspberry Pi arm64 image.
  3. Verify the image checksum.
  4. Identify the target boot device with diskutil list.
  5. Flash with flash --userdata.
  6. Boot the Raspberry Pi.
  7. Wait for cloud-init to finish.
  8. SSH into the node.
  9. Validate hostname, IP address, users, SSH, packages, and disks.
  10. Confirm MinIO disk identity before formatting or mounting.
  11. Add the node to the cluster only after validation succeeds.

docs.title: 10.2 amd64 Node Workflow
docs.text:
Use this workflow for each Intel or AMD bare-metal node.

  1. Download the Ubuntu Server amd64 ISO.
  2. Verify the ISO checksum.
  3. Create a bootable Ubuntu Server installer USB.
  4. Create a NoCloud seed USB from the matching node file.
  5. Boot the amd64 machine with both USB devices attached.
  6. Add autoinstall ds=nocloud to the installer boot line.
  7. Let the installer consume the node-specific user-data.
  8. Reboot after the install completes.
  9. SSH into the node.
  10. Validate hostname, IP address, users, SSH, packages, and disks.
  11. Confirm MinIO disk identity before formatting or mounting.
  12. Add the node to the cluster only after validation succeeds.

For amd64-01, use:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml

For amd64-02, use:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-02.yml

For amd64-03, use:

setup/cloud-config-amd64-03.yml

docs.title: 10.3 amd64 Provisioning Summary
docs.text:
The amd64 flow is:

Ubuntu Server amd64 ISO
  + node-specific NoCloud seed USB
  + autoinstall ds=nocloud
  = provisioned amd64 node

The Raspberry Pi flash --userdata flow is not used for amd64.

The amd64 equivalent is:

copy setup/cloud-config-amd64-01.yml to CIDATA/user-data
boot Ubuntu Server installer with autoinstall ds=nocloud

docs.title: 11. Archived Historical Notes
docs.text:
This section preserves older notes for historical reference only.

The following old command pattern was previously used.

flash \
  --userdata setup/cloud-config-5.yml \
  ~/Downloads/ubuntu-20.04.2-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img

Old Ubuntu 20.04 images and old setup/cloud-config-N.yml files should not be used for new provisioning unless there is a specific compatibility reason.

Avoid old notes such as:

switch to USB drive to trick flash
remove the card, reboot, and then add the card

Those notes may describe a one-time workaround, but they are not reliable provisioning instructions.

docs.title: Appendix A: Useful Validation Commands
docs.text:
This appendix collects frequently used validation commands.

Show attached disks on macOS.

diskutil list

Show Ubuntu block devices.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL

Show whole disks only.

lsblk -dn -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,MODEL,SERIAL

Show filesystems.

lsblk -f

Show the root filesystem.

findmnt /

Show mounted filesystems.

df -h

Show IP addresses.

ip addr

Show routes.

ip route

Show hostname and OS identity.

hostnamectl

Show Ubuntu version.

lsb_release -a

Show cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --long

Wait for cloud-init to finish.

cloud-init status --wait

Check SSH service.

systemctl status ssh --no-pager

Check SSH port reachability.

nc -vz <node-ip> 22

docs.title: Appendix B: Publishing Notes
docs.text:
This document is suitable for a GitHub Pages, MkDocs, or static site publishing pipeline.

Recommended filename:

docs/ubuntu-node-provisioning.md

For Jekyll-style GitHub Pages, this document already includes front matter.

For MkDocs, a matching navigation entry could look like this:

nav:
  - Ubuntu Node Provisioning: ubuntu-node-provisioning.md

For plain GitHub rendering, no additional metadata is required.

docs.title: Appendix C: Source URLs
docs.text:
Ubuntu Raspberry Pi Noble release images:

https://cdimage.ubuntu.com/releases/noble/release/

Ubuntu Server Noble amd64 ISO:

https://releases.ubuntu.com/noble/

Hypriot flash releases:

https://github.com/hypriot/flash/releases

docs.title: Ubuntu Installation and Node Provisioning
docs.text:
This guide describes how to provision Ubuntu nodes for a mixed-architecture homelab or Kubernetes cluster. It supports both Raspberry Pi arm64 machines and Intel/AMD amd64 bare-metal machines.

The goal is to produce repeatable Ubuntu installs while avoiding the two most common provisioning mistakes:

  1. Flashing or installing to the wrong disk.
  2. Assuming Linux disk ordering is stable.

For new installs, prefer Ubuntu 24.04 LTS unless a specific project requires a different release. Raspberry Pi nodes use Ubuntu's preinstalled Raspberry Pi server image. Bare-metal amd64 nodes use the standard Ubuntu Server installer ISO.

This document assumes the flashing workstation is macOS.

All commands are shown in fenced code blocks so they can be selected and copied directly from a browser.

docs.text:

docs.title: 1. Supported Node Types
docs.text:
This provisioning guide supports two node families.

Node Type Architecture Install Method Boot Media Raspberry Pi 4 / Pi 5 arm64 Ubuntu Raspberry Pi preinstalled image plus cloud-init USB SSD or SD card Intel / AMD bare metal amd64 Ubuntu Server ISO or autoinstall SSD or NVMe

Example cluster layout:

arm64-01  Raspberry Pi
arm64-02  Raspberry Pi
arm64-03  Raspberry Pi
arm64-04  Raspberry Pi
arm64-05  Raspberry Pi

amd64-01  Intel / AMD bare metal
amd64-02  Intel / AMD bare metal
amd64-03  Intel / AMD bare metal

Recommended operating system:

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Server

docs.title: 2. General Safety Rules
docs.text:
Provisioning writes directly to disks. Treat every flashing, imaging, and installer step as destructive until proven otherwise.

Never assume any of the following device names are stable:

/dev/disk3
/dev/sda
/dev/sdb
/dev/nvme0n1

These names can change depending on boot order, attached USB devices, drive controllers, BIOS behavior, and kernel discovery order.

Before writing an image, always identify the target disk by:

size
model
vendor
serial number
connection type
whether it appeared after insertion
whether it is removable

For MinIO or other data disks, never rely only on /dev/sda or /dev/sdb. Identify the intended disk using durable characteristics such as:

rotational status
size
model
serial number
existing filesystems
mount status
whether it contains the root filesystem
operator confirmation

docs.title: 3. Recommended Repository Layout
docs.text:
A recommended repository layout is shown below.

setup/
  cloud-config-arm64-01.yml
  cloud-config-arm64-02.yml
  cloud-config-arm64-03.yml
  cloud-config-arm64-04.yml
  cloud-config-arm64-05.yml

  autoinstall-amd64-01/
    user-data
    meta-data

  autoinstall-amd64-02/
    user-data
    meta-data

  autoinstall-amd64-03/
    user-data
    meta-data

docs/
  ubuntu-node-provisioning.md

The arm64 files are intended for Raspberry Pi nodes. The amd64 autoinstall directories are optional and should only be used once disk selection has been tested carefully.

docs.title: 4. Raspberry Pi arm64 Provisioning
docs.text:
Use this section for Raspberry Pi nodes.

Raspberry Pi provisioning uses the Ubuntu preinstalled server image for Raspberry Pi. The cloud-init configuration is injected into the image during flashing.

docs.title: 4.1 Install the Flash Tool on macOS
docs.text:
The Hypriot flash utility can write Ubuntu images and inject a cloud-init user-data file during the flashing process.

Download the flash utility.

curl -LO "https://github.com/hypriot/flash/releases/download/2.5.1/flash"

Make the downloaded file executable.

chmod +x flash

Move the executable into /usr/local/bin.

sudo mv flash /usr/local/bin/flash

Verify that the tool is available.

flash --version

If the command is not found, confirm that /usr/local/bin is in your shell PATH.

echo "$PATH"

docs.title: 4.2 Download the Ubuntu Raspberry Pi Image
docs.text:
Create a local download directory for Raspberry Pi images.

mkdir -p ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi

Move into the download directory.

cd ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi

Download the Ubuntu Raspberry Pi arm64 server image.

curl -LO "https://cdimage.ubuntu.com/releases/noble/release/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz"

Download the checksum file from the same release directory.

curl -LO "https://cdimage.ubuntu.com/releases/noble/release/SHA256SUMS"

The image file should remain compressed as .img.xz. The flash tool can use the compressed image directly.

docs.title: 4.3 Verify the Raspberry Pi Image
docs.text:
Generate the local SHA-256 checksum.

shasum -a 256 ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

Show the expected checksum from Ubuntu's SHA256SUMS file.

grep "ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz" SHA256SUMS

The value from shasum should match the value shown by grep.

Do not flash the image if the checksum does not match.

docs.title: 4.4 Identify the Target Disk on macOS
docs.text:
Before inserting the SD card or USB boot drive, list the disks currently attached to the Mac.

diskutil list

Insert the SD card or USB boot drive.

Then list the disks again.

diskutil list

Identify the newly added disk by comparing the two command outputs.

Example target disk:

/dev/disk3

Do not assume your target disk is /dev/disk3. The correct disk may be /dev/disk2, /dev/disk4, or another value.

The disk shown by flash must match the disk you identified with diskutil list.

docs.title: 4.5 Select the Correct arm64 Cloud-Init File
docs.text:
Use the cloud-init file that matches the Raspberry Pi node being provisioned.

setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml  -> arm64-01
setup/cloud-config-arm64-02.yml  -> arm64-02
setup/cloud-config-arm64-03.yml  -> arm64-03
setup/cloud-config-arm64-04.yml  -> arm64-04
setup/cloud-config-arm64-05.yml  -> arm64-05

Before flashing, inspect the selected file and confirm that the hostname, network settings, users, and SSH keys are correct.

grep -E "hostname|fqdn|192\.168\.2|users|ssh_authorized_keys" \
  setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml

If this command does not show the expected node identity, stop and check the cloud-init file before flashing.

docs.title: 4.6 Flash the Raspberry Pi Boot Device
docs.text:
The following example flashes arm64-01.

flash \
  --userdata setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml \
  ~/Downloads/ubuntu-rpi/ubuntu-24.04.4-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz

During flashing, the tool may prompt for confirmation.

Example prompt:

Is /dev/disk3 correct?

Only answer y if the displayed disk is definitely the intended SD card or USB boot drive.

y

If the disk is not correct, answer n or terminate the command.

docs.title: 4.7 Boot the Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
After flashing completes:

  1. Eject the boot device from macOS.
  2. Insert the SD card or USB drive into the Raspberry Pi.
  3. Connect Ethernet.
  4. Connect power.
  5. Wait for first boot and cloud-init to complete.

The first boot may take several minutes because Ubuntu expands the filesystem, applies cloud-init, configures networking, creates users, installs packages, and starts services.

docs.title: 5. amd64 Bare-Metal Provisioning
docs.text:
Use this section for Intel or AMD bare-metal machines.

The amd64 workflow is different from the Raspberry Pi workflow. Instead of flashing a preinstalled image directly to the boot disk, create a bootable Ubuntu Server installer USB and install Ubuntu onto the machine.

docs.title: 5.1 Download the Ubuntu Server amd64 ISO
docs.text:
Create a local download directory for the Ubuntu Server ISO.

mkdir -p ~/Downloads/ubuntu-amd64

Move into the download directory.

cd ~/Downloads/ubuntu-amd64

Download the Ubuntu Server amd64 ISO.

curl -LO "https://releases.ubuntu.com/noble/ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso"

Download the checksum file.

curl -LO "https://releases.ubuntu.com/noble/SHA256SUMS"

Download the signed checksum file.

curl -LO "https://releases.ubuntu.com/noble/SHA256SUMS.gpg"

docs.title: 5.2 Verify the amd64 ISO
docs.text:
Generate the local SHA-256 checksum.

shasum -a 256 ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso

Show the expected checksum from Ubuntu's SHA256SUMS file.

grep "ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso" SHA256SUMS

The value from shasum should match the value shown by grep.

Do not write the ISO to a USB installer if the checksum does not match.

docs.title: 5.3 Identify the USB Installer Disk on macOS
docs.text:
Insert the USB drive that will become the Ubuntu installer.

Before inserting the USB drive, list attached disks.

diskutil list

After inserting the USB drive, list attached disks again.

diskutil list

Identify the newly added USB drive by size, model, and device name.

Example USB installer disk:

/dev/disk3

Do not assume this value is always correct.

docs.title: 5.4 Create a Bootable USB Installer on macOS
docs.text:
Unmount the USB installer disk.

Replace /dev/disk3 with the disk you identified.

diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk3

Write the Ubuntu Server ISO to the USB drive.

Replace /dev/rdisk3 with the raw disk path that corresponds to your target disk. On macOS, /dev/rdisk3 is the raw version of /dev/disk3.

sudo dd \
  if=ubuntu-24.04.4-live-server-amd64.iso \
  of=/dev/rdisk3 \
  bs=4m \
  status=progress

Flush pending writes.

sync

Eject the USB installer.

diskutil eject /dev/disk3

The dd command overwrites the target disk. If the wrong disk is selected, data loss can occur.

docs.title: 5.5 Install Ubuntu on the amd64 Machine
docs.text:
Insert the USB installer into the target amd64 machine.

Boot the machine and select the USB drive from the boot menu.

During installation:

  1. Choose Ubuntu Server.
  2. Select the intended OS disk.
  3. Do not select the MinIO or data disk as the OS target.
  4. Enable OpenSSH server.
  5. Create the expected administrative user.
  6. Complete the installation.
  7. Reboot after installation finishes.

For machines with both an OS drive and a MinIO drive, the OS should normally be installed on the SSD or NVMe device, not the HDD intended for MinIO.

Example disk layout:

4 TB NVMe       OS / Kubernetes boot disk
1 TB HDD        MinIO data disk

docs.title: 5.6 amd64 Disk Selection Guidance
docs.text:
After the first boot, inspect the disks from Ubuntu.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL

Useful signals:

Signal Meaning ROTA=0 SSD or NVMe ROTA=1 Rotational HDD Large NVMe device Likely OS or fast storage 1 TB rotational disk Likely MinIO disk Mounted / Current boot/root disk Unmounted blank disk Candidate data disk

Do not hard-code Linux disk names.

Avoid assuming these are stable:

/dev/sda
/dev/sdb
/dev/nvme0n1

For MinIO provisioning, identify the intended data disk by combining several signals:

size
rotational status
filesystem state
mount state
model
serial
operator confirmation

docs.title: 6. Optional amd64 Cloud-Init and Autoinstall
docs.text:
Ubuntu autoinstall can make amd64 provisioning repeatable, but it should be used carefully. A bad autoinstall storage configuration can wipe the wrong disk.

For first-pass installs, manual installation is safer. After Ubuntu is installed, use Ansible or a post-install script to apply node-specific configuration.

docs.title: 6.1 Recommended Autoinstall File Layout
docs.text:
Use one autoinstall directory per amd64 node.

setup/
  autoinstall-amd64-01/
    user-data
    meta-data

  autoinstall-amd64-02/
    user-data
    meta-data

  autoinstall-amd64-03/
    user-data
    meta-data

docs.title: 6.2 amd64 Autoinstall Node Mapping
docs.text:
Map each autoinstall configuration to a specific node.

setup/autoinstall-amd64-01/user-data  -> amd64-01
setup/autoinstall-amd64-02/user-data  -> amd64-02
setup/autoinstall-amd64-03/user-data  -> amd64-03

docs.title: 6.3 Autoinstall Safety Warning
docs.text:
Use autoinstall only after disk selection rules have been validated on the actual machine model.

Do not use an autoinstall storage block until you are certain it targets the correct OS disk.

For machines with mixed storage, such as NVMe plus HDD, avoid generic storage rules that blindly select the first available disk.

Bad pattern:

Install to first available disk.

Safer pattern:

Install to the expected SSD or NVMe boot disk after confirming size, model,
serial number, and whether it is already the root target.

docs.title: 7. First-Boot Validation for All Nodes
docs.text:
Run these checks after the first boot on both arm64 and amd64 machines.

These steps confirm that the node is reachable, correctly named, running the expected OS, and using the expected disks.

docs.title: 7.1 Check Network Reachability
docs.text:
Ping the node by IP address.

ping <node-ip>

Example:

ping 192.168.2.51

If the node does not respond, confirm Ethernet, DHCP or static IP configuration, switch connectivity, and whether the machine completed first boot.

docs.title: 7.2 SSH into the Node
docs.text:
Connect with SSH.

ssh dbuddenbaum@<node-ip>

Example:

ssh dbuddenbaum@192.168.2.51

If SSH fails, confirm that OpenSSH was installed and that cloud-init completed.

docs.title: 7.3 Check Cloud-Init Status
docs.text:
Wait for cloud-init to finish.

cloud-init status --wait

Show detailed cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --long

Cloud-init should report that it is done. If it reports an error, review the cloud-init logs before continuing.

docs.title: 7.4 Check Hostname
docs.text:
Show the active hostname and operating system identity.

hostnamectl

Confirm that the hostname matches the expected node name.

Examples:

arm64-01
arm64-02
amd64-01
amd64-02

docs.title: 7.5 Check IP Addresses and Routes
docs.text:
Show assigned IP addresses.

ip addr

Show the routing table.

ip route

Confirm that the node has the expected static IP or DHCP-assigned IP and that a default route exists.

docs.title: 7.6 Check OS Version
docs.text:
Show the Ubuntu release.

lsb_release -a

The release should match the expected Ubuntu version for the cluster.

docs.title: 7.7 Check Block Devices
docs.text:
List block devices with size, rotational status, filesystem, mountpoint, model, and serial number.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL

This is one of the most important validation commands. Use it to confirm which disk is the boot disk and which disk is the candidate MinIO or data disk.

docs.title: 7.8 Check Mounted Filesystems
docs.text:
Show mounted filesystems and available space.

df -h

Confirm that the root filesystem is mounted on the expected boot device.

docs.title: 7.9 Check SSH Service
docs.text:
Show the SSH service status.

systemctl status ssh --no-pager

The service should be active and running.

docs.title: 8. Storage Validation for MinIO Nodes
docs.text:
Before formatting or mounting a MinIO disk, confirm that the selected disk is not the boot disk.

This matters for both Raspberry Pi and amd64 nodes.

Expected storage pattern:

Raspberry Pi nodes:
  boot device: USB SSD or SD card
  MinIO disk: 1 TB HDD

amd64 nodes:
  boot device: SSD or NVMe
  MinIO disk: 1 TB HDD

docs.title: 8.1 Identify the Root Filesystem
docs.text:
Show the mounted root filesystem.

findmnt /

Example output:

TARGET SOURCE         FSTYPE OPTIONS
/      /dev/nvme0n1p2 ext4   rw,relatime

The parent disk of the root filesystem must not be used for MinIO.

In this example, /dev/nvme0n1 is the parent disk of /dev/nvme0n1p2, so /dev/nvme0n1 is the boot disk.

docs.title: 8.2 List Candidate Data Disks
docs.text:
List whole disks without partitions.

lsblk -dn -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,MODEL,SERIAL

Look for the expected MinIO disk by size, rotational status, model, and serial number.

docs.title: 8.3 Show Filesystems
docs.text:
Show existing filesystems.

lsblk -f

A candidate MinIO disk should not contain the active root filesystem.

If a disk already contains data, stop and confirm whether it should be reused, wiped, or excluded.

docs.title: 8.4 Safe MinIO Disk Rule
docs.text:
A disk is a candidate MinIO disk only if all of the following are true:

it is not the root disk
it is the expected size
it is not already mounted
it does not contain the OS filesystem
it matches expected rotational or model characteristics
the operator confirms it

Do not format any disk unless these checks pass.

docs.title: 8.5 Example Manual Confirmation
docs.text:
Use lsblk to inspect the machine.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL

Use findmnt to identify the root filesystem.

findmnt /

Use df to confirm mounted filesystems.

df -h

Only after the boot disk and MinIO disk are clearly identified should a formatting or mounting step be allowed.

docs.title: 9. Troubleshooting
docs.text: This section covers common provisioning failures.

docs.title: 9.1 Cannot SSH into the Node
docs.text:
Check whether the node responds to ping.

ping <node-ip>

Check whether port 22 is reachable.

nc -vz <node-ip> 22

If ping works but SSH fails, check the SSH service from the node console.

sudo systemctl status ssh --no-pager

Check SSH logs.

sudo journalctl -u ssh --no-pager

Check cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --long

Common causes:

cloud-init did not finish
OpenSSH server was not installed
wrong username
wrong SSH key
wrong static IP configuration
node is on the wrong network

docs.title: 9.2 Cloud-Init Did Not Finish
docs.text:
Check cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --long

Check cloud-init service logs.

sudo journalctl -u cloud-init --no-pager

Check final-stage cloud-init logs.

sudo journalctl -u cloud-final --no-pager

Cloud-init issues usually come from YAML formatting errors, package install failures, network configuration errors, or commands in runcmd that failed.

docs.title: 9.3 Wrong Hostname or IP Address
docs.text:
Check the active hostname.

hostnamectl

Check IP addresses.

ip addr

Check routes.

ip route

Check netplan.

cat /etc/netplan/*.yaml

On the provisioning workstation, check the cloud-init file that was used.

grep -E "hostname|fqdn|addresses|gateway4|nameservers" \
  setup/cloud-config-arm64-01.yml

If the wrong cloud-init file was flashed, reflash the node with the correct file.

docs.title: 9.4 Wrong Disk Was Selected
docs.text:
If the wrong disk may have been selected, stop immediately before formatting, mounting, or installing anything else.

Inspect all block devices.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL

Identify the mounted root filesystem.

findmnt /

Check mounted filesystems.

df -h

Do not continue until the root disk and intended data disk are clearly identified.

docs.title: 9.5 Raspberry Pi Does Not Boot from USB
docs.text:
Check the following:

  1. The Raspberry Pi model supports USB boot.
  2. The EEPROM or bootloader is current.
  3. The USB drive is powered correctly.
  4. The image was flashed to the correct device.
  5. Ethernet is connected.
  6. Power is stable.
  7. A monitor shows boot activity.

For Raspberry Pi 4 and newer, USB boot should be handled through the Raspberry Pi bootloader settings. Do not rely on disk-number tricks from the flashing host.

docs.title: 10. Recommended Current Workflows
docs.text: This section summarizes the preferred provisioning path for each node type.

docs.title: 10.1 Raspberry Pi arm64 Node Workflow
docs.text:
Use this workflow for each Raspberry Pi node.

  1. Select the correct setup/cloud-config-arm64-NN.yml file.
  2. Download the Ubuntu Raspberry Pi arm64 image.
  3. Verify the image checksum.
  4. Identify the target boot device with diskutil list.
  5. Flash with flash --userdata.
  6. Boot the Raspberry Pi.
  7. Wait for cloud-init to finish.
  8. SSH into the node.
  9. Validate hostname, IP address, users, SSH, packages, and disks.
  10. Confirm MinIO disk identity before formatting or mounting.
  11. Add the node to the cluster only after validation succeeds.

docs.title: 10.2 amd64 Node Workflow
docs.text:
Use this workflow for each Intel or AMD bare-metal node.

  1. Download the Ubuntu Server amd64 ISO.
  2. Verify the ISO checksum.
  3. Create a bootable USB installer.
  4. Boot the amd64 machine from USB.
  5. Install Ubuntu to the intended boot SSD or NVMe.
  6. Do not install Ubuntu to the MinIO or data HDD.
  7. Reboot.
  8. SSH into the node.
  9. Validate hostname, IP address, users, SSH, packages, and disks.
  10. Confirm MinIO disk identity before formatting or mounting.
  11. Add the node to the cluster only after validation succeeds.

docs.title: 10.3 When to Use Manual Install vs Autoinstall
docs.text:
Use manual installation when:

the machine is new
the disk layout has not been validated
there are multiple disks
you are not sure which disk is the OS disk
you are not sure which disk is the MinIO disk

Use autoinstall only when:

the machine model is known
the disk layout is known
the autoinstall storage configuration has been tested
the risk of wiping the wrong disk has been removed

docs.title: 11. Archived Historical Notes
docs.text:
This section preserves older notes for historical reference only.

The following old command pattern was previously used.

flash \
  --userdata setup/cloud-config-5.yml \
  ~/Downloads/ubuntu-20.04.2-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img

Old Ubuntu 20.04 images and old setup/cloud-config-N.yml files should not be used for new provisioning unless there is a specific compatibility reason.

Avoid old notes such as:

switch to USB drive to trick flash
remove the card, reboot, and then add the card

Those notes may describe a one-time workaround, but they are not reliable provisioning instructions.

docs.title: Appendix A: Useful Validation Commands
docs.text:
This appendix collects frequently used validation commands.

Show attached disks on macOS.

diskutil list

Show Ubuntu block devices.

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,MODEL,SERIAL

Show whole disks only.

lsblk -dn -o NAME,SIZE,ROTA,TYPE,MODEL,SERIAL

Show filesystems.

lsblk -f

Show the root filesystem.

findmnt /

Show mounted filesystems.

df -h

Show IP addresses.

ip addr

Show routes.

ip route

Show hostname and OS identity.

hostnamectl

Show Ubuntu version.

lsb_release -a

Show cloud-init status.

cloud-init status --long

Wait for cloud-init to finish.

cloud-init status --wait

Check SSH service.

systemctl status ssh --no-pager

Check SSH port reachability.

nc -vz <node-ip> 22

docs.title: Appendix B: Publishing Notes
docs.text:
This document is suitable for a GitHub Pages, MkDocs, or static site publishing pipeline.

Recommended filename:

docs/ubuntu-node-provisioning.md

For Jekyll-style GitHub Pages, this document already includes front matter.

For MkDocs, a matching navigation entry could look like this:

nav:
  - Ubuntu Node Provisioning: ubuntu-node-provisioning.md

For plain GitHub rendering, no additional metadata is required.

docs.title: Appendix C: Source URLs
docs.text:
Ubuntu Raspberry Pi Noble release images:

https://cdimage.ubuntu.com/releases/noble/release/

Ubuntu Server Noble amd64 ISO:

https://releases.ubuntu.com/noble/

Hypriot flash releases:

https://github.com/hypriot/flash/releases

docs.title: Centralized Logging Activation, Deployment, Correction, and Runtime Validation Evidence
Executive summary
docs.text:
This validated record documents the activation and deployment of centralized logging as one component of the broader Kalaxy3 observability platform. Loki 18.5.4 and Fluent Bit Collector 1.0.9 are deployed from exact repository locks; Loki and its gateway are ready on amd64-02; one collector is ready on each of seven nodes; the 40 Gi Longhorn volume is attached, healthy, and replicated twice; Grafana loaded and reached the Loki datasource; and recent cluster="kalaxy3" logs from every node are queryable. The record also preserves the partial-deployment failure, repository correction, startup backlog behavior, verification-helper mistakes, final guardrails, and unresolved operational tests.

  • [x] Why includes rationale, alternatives, tradeoffs, and governance constraints.

docs.title: In scope
docs.text:
• Activation of deploy_centralized_logging and publication of commit 9c8b0e68aa742dad796d6871df24faf78f4485aa before cluster mutation.
  • Installation and reconciliation of exact Loki and Fluent Bit Collector chart locks.
  • The partial deployment, datasource failure, repository correction, server-side dry-run, commit 4247387a8062a0a353f5704e40c90b1727881a4a, and successful resumed deployment.
  • Loki and gateway placement, all-node collector readiness, Longhorn storage, Grafana datasource loading and health, Loki queries, all-node stream labels, startup ingestion pressure, and final cluster guardrails.
  • Operator-side verification-helper failures that explain how final evidence collection was hardened.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• Long-term retention-expiry proof for the configured 168h retention period.
  • Longhorn backup, restore, replica-failure, node-loss, and disaster-recovery tests for Loki data.
  • Sustained throughput, capacity, and resource-cost benchmarking under representative workloads.
  • Alerting and SLOs for ingestion rejection, 429 responses, collector buffering, storage pressure, and query latency.
  • Automated repository rollback or deactivation logic; current rollback remains a controlled manual procedure.
  • Acceptance by a named reviewer; status remains validated, not accepted.

docs.title: Nonclaims
docs.text:
• This record does not claim that centralized logging is the entirety of Kalaxy3 observability.
  • It does not claim high availability for the monolithic single-replica Loki process.
  • It does not claim that every historical log line was ingested; old entries were intentionally rejected by Loki's active time windows during startup.
  • It does not claim that the full observability phase is Helm-revision idempotent; kube-prometheus-stack advanced to revision 12 during repeated reconciliation.

docs.title: Problem or opportunity
docs.text: The staged implementation was activation-ready but had not yet been exercised against the live cluster. Activation introduced a real state transition: two new Helm releases, an all-node collector, a persistent logging backend, and a Grafana datasource. The first live run exposed a controller/target dependency mismatch after the logging workloads were already installed.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Proceed through secured checkpoints: first publish the gate activation without touching the cluster; then deploy through the repository observability phase; preserve the partial state when datasource provisioning failed; correct the repository instead of installing an ad hoc Python dependency on arm64-01; resume the same phase; and require runtime validation before declaring completion.

docs.title: Decision drivers
docs.text:
• Preserve repository authority and controller portability.
  • Avoid disguising a partial deployment as either total success or total failure.
  • Reuse the existing K3s CLI authority already available on the execution node.
  • Keep Loki and Fluent Bit on exact, approved chart locks.
  • Require evidence of the actual data path, not only pod readiness.
  • Retain failed paths that explain the final implementation and validation method.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Alternative Advantages Disadvantages or risks Decision Install the Python Kubernetes client globally on arm64-01 Minimal task rewrite Adds a remote package dependency not established by the repository and creates controller drift rejected Run the datasource task only from the macOS controller Existing Python environment Splits phase execution authority and requires controller-specific kubeconfig handling rejected Use repository-established k3s kubectl apply on the execution host No new dependency, simple, auditable, works with existing K3s authority Changed-state detection must parse command output accepted Roll back Loki and Fluent Bit immediately after datasource failure Restores pre-deployment state Discards healthy installed work and adds unnecessary storage churn rejected Ignore startup 429 and old-entry errors Faster closure Could hide persistent loss or an undersized ingestion path rejected Raise Loki limits immediately May accelerate backlog drain Changes capacity policy before measuring whether startup pressure is transient deferred

docs.title: Tradeoffs and consequences
docs.text:
• A single-replica monolithic Loki is economical and simple, but not process-highly-available.
  • Retained Longhorn storage provides disk replication, but does not replace tested backup and restore.
  • The all-node collector provides broad coverage, but a first start can replay significant local backlog and transiently exceed ingestion limits.
  • auth_enabled: false simplifies internal single-tenant operation, but makes network isolation and Grafana access controls important.
  • Re-running the broad observability phase reconciles desired state but advanced the Prometheus stack Helm revision even when its locked chart stayed unchanged.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
Assumption ID Assumption Risk if false Validation plan ASM-001 The final five-minute error-free collector window is representative of steady state. Future restarts may replay enough backlog to trigger sustained 429 responses or dropped old records. Observe restart behavior and alert on collector output errors and Loki rejected samples. ASM-002 Seven-day retention and compaction behave as configured on filesystem storage. Storage may fill or records may persist or disappear outside policy. Measure volume growth and verify expiry after more than 168 hours. ASM-003 Two Longhorn replicas provide adequate durability for this homelab workload. Simultaneous node or disk loss could exceed protection. Add recurring backups and execute restore and replica-failure tests. ASM-004 Internal cluster network trust is sufficient while Loki authentication is disabled. A compromised pod could query cluster logs. Add or validate NetworkPolicy and least-privilege access before broader tenancy.

These assumptions prevent accepted status until the owner and reviewer explicitly accept the residual risks or the listed tests close them.

docs.title: Expected change
docs.text:
• Install exactly one locked Loki release and one locked Fluent Bit Collector release.
  • Schedule Loki and its gateway on the unique intended node.
  • Run one collector on every node.
  • Provision the Grafana datasource.
  • Preserve Longhorn-backed Loki storage and return queryable logs.

docs.title: Observed change
docs.text: The first run installed both logging releases but stopped at datasource provisioning (EV-002). The corrected rerun left both logging releases at revision 1, created the datasource, and completed without failure (EV-004). Runtime checks then passed for topology, storage, datasource health, ingestion, all-node coverage, and final guardrails (EV-005 through EV-011).

docs.title: Failed or superseded paths
docs.text:
• kubernetes.core.k8s on arm64-01 failed because /usr/bin/python3 lacked the Python Kubernetes library. Installing the library ad hoc was rejected; k3s kubectl apply became the accepted repository path.
  • A revision-report helper raised a shell-quoting NameError; no observability phase ran in that attempt.
  • A Secret-reading helper used Python standard input for both script and JSON and raised JSONDecodeError; the deployment itself had already completed through datasource creation.
  • A dictionary-key quoting helper raised KeyError; it was read-only.
  • Bash indirect expansion pasted into zsh failed during parsing with event not found; no command ran.
  • The final verification explicitly invoked Bash, used file-backed JSON, and retained cleanup traps.
